narrative:
The model estimated a 91.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and that high estimated risk is why your law school application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty, but it means the model saw your profile as much closer to students who did not pass than to students who passed.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank: you are in the lowest tenth of your class, while accepted students average around the sixth tenth. That very low rank strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second-most influential factor and showed the same pattern: you were in the lowest tenth, compared with an average near the sixth tenth, which also increased the predicted risk. Your LSAT score of 37 was essentially at the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it slightly pushed toward passing, but it was only the third-most influential factor and could not offset the concerns about your class rank.

To strengthen a future application, ask admissions what specifically concerned them, consider retaking the LSAT only if you can meaningfully improve, complete additional rigorous coursework that demonstrates law-school readiness, and seek academic advising. You may also apply to other programs and build legal or professional experience while addressing the academic record that drove this decision.
